content: The use of anthracyclines in cancer treatment is often limited due to the risk of cardiotoxicity. To address this issue, various anthracycline derivatives have been studied to determine their potential to reduce cardiotoxic effects. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the occurrence of cardiotoxicity associated with different anthracycline derivatives in cancer patients. The search included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to mid-2009. Additional sources, including reference lists, conference proceedings, and ongoing trial databases, were also reviewed. The analysis focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different anthracycline derivatives in both adult and pediatric cancer patients. Two reviewers independently selected studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data, including information on adverse effects. Five RCTs were identified that compared epirubicin and doxorubicin at equivalent doses, involving a total of 1,036 patients. The meta-analysis did not reveal a statistically significant difference in the incidence of clinical heart failure between the two treatment groups (relative risk [RR] = 0.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.12 to 1.11). However, there was a suggestion of a lower rate of clinical heart failure in patients treated with epirubicin. Two additional RCTs, involving 521 patients, compared liposomal-encapsulated doxorubicin with conventional doxorubicin. The meta-analysis demonstrated a significantly lower rate of clinical heart failure (RR = 0.20, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.75) and combined clinical and subclinical heart failure (RR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.59) in patients receiving liposomal-encapsulated doxorubicin. It is important to note that in one of these studies, patients in the liposomal-encapsulated doxorubicin group received a higher cumulative dose of anthracyclines compared to those in the conventional doxorubicin group. For other combinations of anthracycline derivatives, only one RCT was identified (comparing epirubicin with liposomal-encapsulated doxorubicin), or no RCTs were available. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to favor either epirubicin or doxorubicin when administered at the same dose. However, based on the available evidence, liposomal-encapsulated doxorubicin appears to be preferable to conventional doxorubicin in adult patients with solid tumors due to its lower cardiotoxicity. No conclusions could be drawn regarding the effects of these treatments in pediatric patients or in individuals with leukemia. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence to make definitive conclusions about the cardiotoxicity of other anthracycline derivatives. Further research is needed to address these gaps in knowledge.
